learn.hook: Ask five people what 'a better life' means and you may get five different answers — and some of them may even clash!
points: Development means progress, but people do not all want the same things. Each person's development goals depend on their life situation.
A landless rural labourer may want more days of work and better wages; a prosperous farmer may want higher prices for crops; a girl in a city may want the same freedom as her brother.
Goals can conflict: a big dam may give electricity to industries and cities, but it may submerge villages and force families to move. Development for one group can mean loss for another.
People want more income, but they also seek non-material things: equal treatment, freedom, security, respect from others and friendship.

Some things money cannot buy for one person alone: a pollution-free environment, medicines that are not adulterated, or protection from infectious diseases. These usually need the whole community or the government to act together.

example.q: Think it through: Arjun gets two job offers. Job A pays ₹5,000 more per month but is in a faraway city with no job security. Job B pays a little less, is close to his family and is permanent. What should he consider?
steps: Income matters: Job A gives more money each month.
Non-income factors also matter: job security, time with family, a safe working atmosphere and chances to learn.
Job B offers security and family support, which money alone cannot buy.
So the choice depends on Arjun's own goals — there is no single answer that is right for everyone.
example.answer: Both income and non-income goals matter; the 'better' job depends on what Arjun values most.

learn.reallife: When your family discusses moving to a new city for a job, they think about salary, but also schools, safety, distance from grandparents and the neighbourhood — that is development thinking in action.

games.title: Development goals: true or false?
items: Different people can have different development goals.
Goals depend on each person's life situation, so they differ.
What is development for one person can be harmful for another.
A dam can power factories but displace the villagers whose land goes under water.
People care only about earning more money.
People also want freedom, equality, security and respect.
A clean environment is something one family can easily buy for itself.
Clean air and water need collective action by the community or government.
Job security can matter as much as salary when choosing a job.
Many people value a secure, permanent job along with income.
Equal treatment and respect are examples of non-material goals.
They cannot be measured in rupees but are important for a good life.

quiz.q: Which development goal would a landless rural labourer most likely have?
options: Higher support prices for the crops he grows
More days of work and better wages
quiz.explain: A landless labourer does not own land or a factory; he depends on wages, so more work and better pay are his main goals.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the goals of a labourer with those of a landowning farmer or industrialist

quiz.q: A dam will give electricity to cities but will submerge several villages. What does this show about development?
options: Development goals can conflict: one group's gain may be another's loss
Dams are always bad for everyone
Development goals are the same for all people
quiz.explain: City users and industries gain power, while villagers lose their homes and land, so their goals clash.
quiz.mistake: Assumes everyone gains equally from a development project

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-material development goal?
options: Being treated with respect and equality
quiz.explain: Respect and equal treatment cannot be bought or measured in money, so they are non-material goals.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only things that can be bought count as goals

quiz.q: Which of these is hardest for one family to buy with its own money?
quiz.explain: Clean air and water depend on what everyone around does, so they need community or government action, not one family's spending.
quiz.mistake: Believes money alone can buy every good thing in life

quiz.q: Dengue spreads through mosquitoes breeding in stagnant water. What is the most effective protection for a colony?
options: Each family buying an expensive gadget for itself
Everyone together clearing stagnant water across the whole colony
Ignoring it, since only some houses are affected
quiz.explain: Mosquitoes fly from house to house, so protection works only when the whole community acts together.
quiz.mistake: Thinks private spending can replace collective action

quiz.q: Priya is choosing between two jobs with equal pay. Which factor is a non-income reason to prefer one job?
options: A safe working atmosphere and job security
quiz.explain: Safety and security are not about money but still make a job better. The other options are all about income.
quiz.mistake: Counts money-related benefits as non-income factors

quiz.q: Why do different people have different notions of development?
options: Because only rich people think about development
Because development has one fixed meaning for everyone
Because people's life situations, needs and hopes are different
Because the government decides every person's goals
quiz.explain: People in different situations — farmers, workers, students, business owners — need and hope for different things.
quiz.mistake: Assumes development means the same thing for all

quiz.q: Which pair shows conflicting development goals?
options: A student wants good teachers; a parent wants a good school
A farmer wants rain; another farmer wants rain too
A patient wants a nearby hospital; a doctor wants a well-equipped hospital
An industrialist wants a new factory on farmland; farmers want to keep farming that land
quiz.explain: The same land cannot be used for both, so the industrialist's goal and the farmers' goal clash.
quiz.mistake: Confuses similar or matching goals with conflicting ones

teach.ask: Gappu flaps his wings: 'Development just means getting more money, right? Why would anyone want anything else?'
teach.praise: Wow! So development is about money AND freedom, respect and security — and my goals may even clash with someone else's. Chirp-tastic!
teach.nudge: But do all people want the same things? And is money the only thing people care about?

topics.title: Per capita income: comparing countries and states

learn.hook: A cricket team's total runs don't tell you how good each batter is — and a country's total income doesn't tell you how well-off each person is!
points: Income is the most common way to compare countries: a country with more income is usually thought to be more developed, because people can buy more of what they need.
Total income is not a fair comparison, because countries have different populations. So we use average income: total income of the country ÷ its total population.

Average income is also called per capita income ('per head'). The World Bank's World Development Report uses per capita income to classify countries; it places India among low middle income countries.
An average can hide inequality: two countries can have the same average income, but in one everyone earns about the same while in the other a few are very rich and most are poor.
So per capita income is useful but incomplete — it says nothing about how income is shared or about health and education.

example.q: Think it through: Village Sundarpur has 5 families earning ₹9,000, ₹11,000, ₹10,000, ₹9,500 and ₹10,500 a month. Village Rampur has 5 families earning ₹1,000, ₹1,000, ₹1,000, ₹1,000 and ₹46,000. Compare them.
steps: Both averages are equal, but in Rampur four families earn only ₹1,000 each.
Sundarpur's income is shared far more equally, so most people would prefer to live there.
example.answer: Same average (₹10,000), but Sundarpur is more equal — averages hide how income is distributed.

learn.reallife: If a class's average marks are 70, it could be that everyone scored about 70 — or that some scored 100 and some scored 40. You need more than the average to know the full story.

quiz.mistake: Gives the total instead of dividing by the number of families

quiz.q: Why is total income NOT a useful way to compare two countries?
options: Because total income cannot be measured
Because rich countries hide their income
Because total income is always the same for all countries
Because countries have different populations, so total income tells little about what an average person earns
quiz.explain: A big country may have a huge total income but also a huge population, so we must look at income per person.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that population size differs between countries

quiz.q: Which report classifies countries mainly by their per capita income?
options: World Development Report of the World Bank
Annual report of the Reserve Bank of India
Report of the World Trade Organisation
quiz.explain: The World Bank's World Development Report uses per capita income. The UNDP's report uses the Human Development Index instead.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the World Bank's report with UNDP's Human Development Report

quiz.q: In the World Bank's classification, in which group does India fall?
quiz.explain: India's per capita income places it among the low middle income countries.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a large total income makes India a high-income country

quiz.q: An island has a total yearly income of ₹90,00,000 and 300 people. What is its per capita income?
quiz.mistake: Makes a place-value slip while dividing large numbers

quiz.q: Country P and Country Q have the same average income. In P, everyone earns about the same; in Q, one person is very rich and the rest are poor. Where would most people prefer to live?
options: Country P, because income is shared more equally
Country Q, because it has a very rich person
Either one, since the averages are equal
Country Q, because inequality raises everyone's income
quiz.explain: With equal averages, the country with fairer distribution gives most people a better income.
quiz.mistake: Believes equal averages mean equal living conditions

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of using only per capita income to measure development?
options: It is too difficult to calculate
It does not show how income is distributed or how healthy and educated people are
It is always higher than total income
quiz.explain: Per capita income is an average; it hides inequality and says nothing about health, education or other facilities.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the average gives the complete picture of people's lives

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'My forest has more total nuts than the next forest, so all my bird friends must be richer. Right? What is per capita income?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Divide total income by the number of people to get the average — but an average can hide that some are rich and many are poor. Got it!
teach.nudge: But what do we divide the total income by? And can an average tell us whether income is shared fairly?

learn.hook: Would you rather live where people earn a little more — or where babies survive, children study and the hospital is close by?
points: Infant Mortality Rate (IMR): the number of children who die before the age of one year for every 1000 live births in that year. Literacy rate: the proportion of literate people in the 7 years and above age group. Net attendance ratio: children aged 14 and 15 attending school as a percentage of all children of that age.

A state with lower per capita income can still do better in health and education. The textbook shows Kerala with a low infant mortality rate and high literacy because it has adequate basic health and education facilities.

Many important needs are best met by public facilities provided collectively: schools, health centres, and ration shops of the Public Distribution System. Collective provision is often cheaper and reaches more people.

The UNDP's Human Development Report compares countries by their educational levels, health status and per capita income. Its Human Development Index (HDI) uses life expectancy at birth, mean years of schooling, expected years of schooling and gross national income per capita.

Sustainability: development should continue for future generations too. Groundwater is a renewable resource refilled by rain, but it gets used up if we pump it faster than it is refilled. Crude oil is non-renewable — its stock is limited and will run out.

example.q: Think it through: State X has a higher per capita income than State Y, but State X's IMR is 30 while State Y's IMR is 6. Which state has better health conditions, and why might this happen?
steps: IMR counts infant deaths per 1000 live births, so a lower IMR is better.
State Y loses 6 babies out of every 1000, State X loses 30 — State Y is far better.
Money in people's pockets cannot by itself buy vaccination drives, clean water or nearby health centres.
State Y has probably invested in public health and education facilities.
example.answer: State Y, because it has a much lower IMR; good public health facilities matter, not just income.

learn.reallife: When an anganwadi in your area gives free check-ups and nutrition to small children, or a government school gives midday meals, that is public provision improving human development.

quiz.q: What does the Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) measure?
options: Number of children born per 1000 people
Number of children who die before age one per 1000 live births in a year
Number of children who go to school
Number of children below age five in a family
quiz.explain: IMR counts deaths of babies before their first birthday out of every 1000 live births in that year.
quiz.mistake: Confuses mortality (deaths) with birth rate

quiz.q: Literacy rate measures the proportion of literate people in which age group?
quiz.explain: Literacy rate is calculated for the population aged 7 years and above.
quiz.mistake: Guesses the school-starting or adult age instead of 7 years

quiz.q: In a district, there were 4000 live births in a year and 60 of these babies died before their first birthday. What is the IMR?
quiz.explain: IMR is per 1000 live births: 60 ÷ 4000 × 1000 = 15.
steps: Deaths per birth = 60 ÷ 4000
quiz.mistake: Gives the raw number of deaths instead of the rate per 1000

quiz.q: Which organisation publishes the Human Development Report?
quiz.explain: The Human Development Report is published by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
quiz.mistake: Confuses UNDP with the World Bank, which publishes the World Development Report

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT used in calculating the Human Development Index?
quiz.explain: HDI combines health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income. Cars owned are not part of it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks owning luxury goods is an HDI indicator

quiz.q: According to the textbook, why does Kerala have a low infant mortality rate?
options: Because it has the highest per capita income in India
Because few babies are born there
Because it has adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities
quiz.explain: Kerala's good basic health and education facilities, not just income, keep its IMR low.
quiz.mistake: Assumes good health always comes from higher income

quiz.q: Groundwater is a renewable resource. Why can it still run short?
options: Because it is used faster than rain can refill it
Because groundwater cannot be used for farming
quiz.explain: A renewable resource is refilled by nature, but if we pump out more than is refilled, it gets overused and falls.
quiz.mistake: Thinks renewable means a resource can never run out

quiz.q: What does 'sustainable development' mean?
options: Development that meets today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
Development that uses up resources as fast as possible
Development that stops all use of natural resources
quiz.explain: Sustainability means development should continue for future generations, so resources and the environment must be protected.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sustainability means either using everything now or using nothing at all

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'If a state has more money, it must have healthier babies, right? And why do grown-ups keep saying sustainable?'
teach.praise: Hooray! So development also means health, education and public facilities — measured by HDI — and it must last for the future too!
teach.nudge: Is income enough? What about health, schooling and resources for the future?

topics.title: Primary, secondary and tertiary sectors and GDP

learn.hook: Your morning cup of chai passes through all three sectors of the economy before it reaches your hands!
points: Primary sector: producing goods by directly using natural resources — agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry and mining. It is also called the agriculture and related sector.
Secondary sector: changing natural products into other forms through manufacturing — sugar from sugarcane, cloth from cotton, bricks from clay. It is also called the industrial sector.

Tertiary sector: activities that support the other two and produce services rather than goods — transport, storage, communication, banking and trade, plus services of teachers, doctors, lawyers and IT workers. It is also called the service sector.
The sectors depend on each other: a farmer needs transport and a market, and a textile mill needs cotton from farmers.

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. Only final goods are counted, because the value of intermediate goods (like cotton used to make cloth) is already included in the final good's value — counting both would be double counting.

example.q: Think it through: A farmer sells sugarcane worth ₹40 to a mill. The mill makes sugar and sells it for ₹70 to a sweet shop. The sweet shop uses it to make jalebis and sells them to customers for ₹200. How much is added to GDP?
steps: Sugarcane and sugar are intermediate goods here — they are used up in making something else.
The jalebis sold to customers are the final good, worth ₹200.
The ₹200 price already includes the value of the sugar and sugarcane used.
Adding 40 + 70 + 200 = ₹310 would count the sugarcane and sugar more than once.
example.answer: ₹200 — only the value of the final good is counted.

learn.reallife: The tea leaves are plucked in Assam's gardens (primary), processed and packed in a factory (secondary), and carried by trucks and sold at your local kirana shop (tertiary).

quiz.q: Fishing belongs to which sector of the economy?
quiz.explain: Fishing directly uses a natural resource, so it is a primary sector activity.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the type of activity with the conditions of employment

quiz.q: Making sugar from sugarcane is an activity of which sector?
quiz.explain: Sugarcane, a natural product, is changed into sugar through manufacturing — a secondary sector activity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything related to crops belongs to the primary sector

quiz.q: Why is the tertiary sector also called the service sector?
options: Because it manufactures goods in factories
Because it produces services rather than goods
Because only the government runs it
Because it uses natural resources directly
quiz.explain: Transport, banking, teaching and trade do not produce goods themselves; they provide services.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the tertiary sector with manufacturing

quiz.q: Which is the correct meaning of GDP?
options: The total income earned by Indians living abroad
The value of all intermediate goods produced in a year
The total amount of money printed in a year
The value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year
quiz.explain: GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced within the country in one year.
quiz.mistake: Includes intermediate goods or confuses GDP with money supply

quiz.q: A farmer sells cotton for ₹50 to a mill, the mill sells yarn for ₹80 to a weaver, and the weaver sells cloth to customers for ₹150. What value is added to GDP?
quiz.explain: Only the final good, the cloth worth ₹150, is counted. Its price already includes the cotton and yarn.
steps: Cotton and yarn are intermediate goods
Cloth sold to customers is the final good
Value counted = ₹150
quiz.mistake: Adds the values at every stage, which is double counting

quiz.q: Which of these is an intermediate good?
options: A packet of biscuits bought by a family
A bicycle bought by a student
Flour bought by a biscuit factory to make biscuits
quiz.explain: The flour is used up in making biscuits, so it is an intermediate good. The others are final goods or services used by consumers.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a good's type, not its use, decides whether it is intermediate

quiz.q: Why are only final goods counted in GDP?
options: Because the value of intermediate goods is already included in the final value, so counting them would be double counting
Because intermediate goods have no value
Because the government does not allow it
quiz.explain: The price of the final good already covers the intermediate goods used to make it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks intermediate goods are worthless instead of already included

quiz.q: If all truck drivers go on strike, farmers cannot send vegetables to cities. What does this show?
options: The primary sector does not need any other sector
Farming belongs to the secondary sector
The three sectors depend on each other
quiz.explain: Farmers (primary) need transport (tertiary) to reach markets, so the sectors are interdependent.
quiz.mistake: Treats each sector as working in isolation

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'A farmer, a factory and a bank — how are they different? And what is this GDP thing?'
teach.praise: Yay! Primary uses nature, secondary manufactures, tertiary gives services — and GDP counts only final goods and services. Super clear!
teach.nudge: Which sector uses natural resources and which one gives services? And which goods does GDP count?

learn.hook: Five people working on a field that needs only three — everyone looks busy, but is everyone really needed?
points: In the early stages of development, the primary sector was the most important. As farming improved and produced more food, people moved to manufacturing and the secondary sector became most important. In developed countries today, the tertiary sector is the most important.
In India, production has grown in all three sectors, but most in the tertiary sector, which has become the largest producing sector, replacing the primary sector.

Reasons for tertiary growth: basic services like hospitals, schools, post offices, police, courts and banks are needed; growing farms and factories need more transport, trade and storage; rising incomes create demand for services like eating out, tourism and private schools; new IT-based services have grown fast. But many tertiary workers, like small shopkeepers and repair workers, still earn very little.

Jobs did not shift the same way: the primary sector is still the largest employer in India, even though its share in GDP is much smaller. The secondary and tertiary sectors have not created enough jobs.

Disguised unemployment (underemployment): more people work than are needed, so if some leave, output does not fall. It is common in farming and also among urban casual workers who have work only part of the time.

More jobs can come from irrigation, rural roads, storage and cheap credit, agro-processing units, tourism, health and education. The textbook also describes MGNREGA 2005, a law that guaranteed 100 days of work in a year to rural people who needed and could do work, with an unemployment allowance if work was not given. Update: in December 2025 a new law, the Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-G RAM G), was passed to replace MGNREGA from 1 July 2026; it guarantees 125 days of wage work in a year. For your exam, learn MGNREGA as the textbook describes it.

example.q: Think it through: Meena's family of 5 works on a small 2-hectare farm. The farm needs only 3 workers. Two family members find jobs in a nearby town and production stays the same. What does this show?
steps: Before, 5 people worked but only 3 were really needed.
When 2 left, output did not fall, so their labour was adding nothing extra.
This is disguised unemployment: people appear employed but are not fully productive.
The 2 members can now add to the family income from the town, so the family is better off.
example.answer: 2 members were disguisedly unemployed; moving them to other work raises total income.

learn.reallife: On a city street, many painters and plumbers wait at a chowk every morning for daily work; many get work only on some days — another form of underemployment.

quiz.explain: Production grew fastest in the tertiary sector, which replaced the primary sector as the largest producer.

quiz.q: Which sector still employs the largest number of workers in India?
quiz.explain: Most workers are still in the primary sector, mainly agriculture, although its share in GDP is much smaller.

quiz.q: Which is a reason for the growth of the tertiary sector in India?

Farming has completely stopped in India
quiz.explain: As incomes rise, people spend more on services, which helps the tertiary sector grow.
quiz.mistake: Picks an exaggerated claim instead of a real cause

quiz.q: What is disguised unemployment?
options: When workers are on a paid holiday
When people have no work at all and say so openly
When workers move abroad for jobs
When more people work than needed, so some are not really productive
quiz.explain: In disguised unemployment, everyone seems to be working, but removing some workers would not reduce output.
quiz.mistake: Confuses hidden underemployment with open unemployment

quiz.q: Historically, as countries developed, which sector became the most important after the primary sector?
quiz.explain: Better farming freed people to work in manufacturing, so the secondary sector became most important next; the tertiary sector rose later.
quiz.mistake: Skips the industrial stage and jumps to services

quiz.q: As described in the textbook, MGNREGA 2005 guaranteed rural people who needed work how many days of employment in a year?
quiz.explain: The textbook explains that MGNREGA 2005 guaranteed 100 days of employment in a year, and an unemployment allowance if work was not provided. (Update: from 1 July 2026 MGNREGA is replaced by the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, which guarantees 125 days.)
quiz.mistake: Guesses a number instead of recalling the 100-day guarantee

quiz.q: Which step would best create more jobs in a village where farmers grow only one crop a year?
options: Banning farmers from selling in towns
Building wells or canals for irrigation
quiz.explain: Irrigation lets farmers grow a second crop, which needs more workers and creates more jobs.
quiz.mistake: Does not link irrigation to more farm work

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'If services now make the most money in India, then most people must work in services. Right? And what is disguised unemployment?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Services produce the most, but farming still employs the most — and many farm workers are disguisedly unemployed. Brilliant!
teach.nudge: Which sector produces most and which employs most? And what happens to output when the extra workers leave?

learn.hook: Two people both work 8 hours a day — one gets paid leave and a pension, the other can lose the job tomorrow. What's the difference?
points: Organised sector: enterprises or places of work with regular terms of employment. They are registered by the government and must follow laws such as the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and Shops and Establishments Act. (Update: since 21 November 2025 the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and many other central labour laws have been combined into four new Labour Codes; the idea of the organised sector stays the same.)

Organised-sector workers get job security, fixed working hours, extra pay for overtime, paid leave, payment during holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits and often a pension after retirement.

Unorganised sector: small, scattered units largely outside government control. Rules exist but are often not followed. Jobs are low-paid and irregular, with no overtime pay, paid leave or sick leave, and workers can be removed without reason.

Many people work in the unorganised sector: in villages — landless labourers, small and marginal farmers, sharecroppers and artisans; in towns — casual construction workers, street vendors, head-load workers, garment workers in small units and rag pickers.
Unorganised workers need protection: the government can fix minimum wages and working hours, and help small units with cheap loans, raw materials and marketing.

example.q: Think it through: Sunil works in a registered car-parts factory with a written contract, paid leave and provident fund. His cousin Raju works at a small roadside workshop, is paid in cash daily and gets nothing when he falls ill. Which sector does each belong to?
steps: Sunil's job has regular terms, is registered and gives benefits like paid leave and provident fund.
These are features of the organised sector.
Raju's job is irregular, has no leave or security and follows no formal rules.
These are features of the unorganised sector.
example.answer: Sunil — organised sector; Raju — unorganised sector.

learn.reallife: The person who sells bhutta near your school, the helper at a small dhaba and the daily-wage worker building a house are mostly in the unorganised sector; a bank clerk or a railway engineer is in the organised sector.

quiz.q: The textbook lists laws about workers that organised-sector enterprises must follow. Which of these is one of them?

quiz.mistake: Picks a real law that is not about employment conditions

quiz.q: Which group of workers is mostly found in the unorganised sector in rural areas?
quiz.explain: Landless labourers, small farmers, sharecroppers and artisans usually have irregular work and no benefits.

quiz.q: Which government step would most directly help small units in the unorganised sector?

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Both my uncles work all day. One gets paid holidays and one doesn't. Why? Explain organised and unorganised sectors!'
teach.praise: Chirp! Organised jobs are registered and follow rules with benefits; unorganised jobs are irregular with no security. You nailed it!
teach.nudge: Which sector follows government rules? What benefits do workers there get that others don't?

learn.hook: The train you ride and the biscuit you munch on it are made by two very different kinds of owners!
points: Sectors can also be classified by who owns the assets. In the public sector, the government owns most of the assets and provides the services, like the Indian Railways and post offices.
In the private sector, assets are owned and services delivered by private individuals or companies.
The private sector's main motive is to earn profits. The public sector's aim is not just profit but public welfare; the government raises money through taxes to pay for its services.

Some things need huge spending that the private sector will not provide at a reasonable cost: roads, bridges, railways, harbours, generating electricity and irrigation through dams. It is also hard to collect money from thousands of users, so the government provides these.

The government also supports private activity — for example, it sells electricity at low rates to industries, and buys wheat and rice from farmers at a fair price, stores them and sells them at lower prices through ration shops. It also has a duty to provide health and education facilities for all.

example.q: Think it through: Why would a private company not want to build a long bridge connecting a few villages across a river?
steps: Building a bridge costs a huge amount of money.
Collecting a fee from every villager who walks or cycles across would be very hard.
The private company could not earn enough profit, so it would not invest.
The government, which aims at public welfare and collects taxes, can build it for everyone.
example.answer: Because it is too costly and unprofitable for a private company; the government builds it for public welfare.

learn.reallife: When your family buys rice and wheat at a lower price from the local ration shop, you see the government supporting both farmers and consumers.

games.title: Three ways to classify
pairs: Main motive of the private sector
Main aim of the public sector

quiz.q: On what basis are sectors classified as public and private?

quiz.q: Why does the government usually build roads, bridges and dams?

quiz.explain: These projects cost a lot and are hard to charge every user for, so the government provides them for public welfare.
quiz.mistake: Thinks such projects are left to the government because they are highly profitable

quiz.q: The government buys wheat from farmers at a fair price and sells it at a lower price through ration shops. Whom does this help?

quiz.mistake: Misses that the scheme supports both sides

quiz.q: A chain of hospitals is owned by a group of private shareholders. Which sector does it belong to?

quiz.q: Dividing the economy into organised and unorganised sectors is based on:
quiz.explain: Organised and unorganised sectors differ in terms of employment — rules, security and benefits.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Who owns the train I ride and the biscuit factory? Why doesn't one company just build all the roads?'
teach.praise: Hooray! The public sector is owned by the government for public welfare; the private sector is owned by people or companies for profit. Perfect!
teach.nudge: Who owns each sector, and what is each one's main aim — profit or welfare?

topics.title: Money as a medium of exchange

learn.hook: Imagine trying to buy a samosa by offering the shopkeeper a pair of socks — and he wants a cricket ball instead!
points: In a barter system, goods are exchanged directly for goods. It needs a double coincidence of wants: what one person wants to sell must be exactly what the other wants to buy, and the other way round.
Money acts as a medium of exchange — an in-between item in every exchange. A person sells goods for money and uses that money to buy what she needs, so double coincidence is no longer needed.
Many things have served as money: in early times Indians used grains and cattle; later came metallic coins of gold, silver and copper; today we use paper notes and coins.

Modern currency has no use of its own; it is accepted because the government authorises it. In India, the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government, and by law the rupee cannot be refused for settling payments in India.

People also keep money as deposits in banks and earn interest. Demand deposits can be withdrawn whenever needed. A cheque is a paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the account to the person named on it. Because demand deposits are widely accepted for payment, they share the essential features of money.

Banks keep only a small part of their deposits as cash and lend most of the rest. They charge a higher interest rate on loans than they pay on deposits; this difference is the main source of a bank's income.

example.q: Think it through: A shoemaker in Agra wants wheat. A wheat farmer wants cloth, not shoes. Can they trade by barter? How does money help?
steps: The shoemaker wants wheat, but the farmer does not want shoes.
So there is no double coincidence of wants and barter fails.
With money, the shoemaker sells shoes to anyone who wants them and gets money.
He then pays the farmer money for wheat, and the farmer uses it to buy cloth.
example.answer: Barter fails without double coincidence; money as a medium of exchange solves the problem.

learn.reallife: When your parent pays the vegetable seller by cheque, card or a phone payment from a bank account, the money moves out of a bank deposit — deposits work just like cash.

games.title: How exchange changed over time
games.prompt: Put these in the order they came into use
items: Direct exchange of goods for goods (barter)

items.text: Barter needs a double ___ of wants.

quiz.q: What does 'double coincidence of wants' mean?

Both people have the same amount of money

quiz.explain: In barter, each person must want exactly what the other is offering for the exchange to happen.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it means both people want the same item

quiz.q: How does money solve the problem of double coincidence of wants?
options: By making everyone produce the same goods
By acting as a medium of exchange that everyone accepts

quiz.mistake: Does not see money as the 'in-between' item in exchange

quiz.q: Who issues currency notes in India?
options: Reserve Bank of India, on behalf of the central government

quiz.mistake: Thinks any bank or state government can print notes

options: Because it is made of special gold paper

quiz.explain: Modern currency is accepted because it is authorised by the government; by law, the rupee cannot be refused in India.
quiz.mistake: Thinks money's value comes from the material it is made of

quiz.q: Why are some bank deposits called demand deposits?
options: Because the bank demands money from the depositor
Because they can be withdrawn whenever the depositor wants
Because they earn no interest at all

quiz.mistake: Reverses who makes the demand

quiz.q: What is a cheque?
options: A paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from a person's account to the person named on it
A coin issued by the government
quiz.explain: A cheque tells the bank to transfer money from the account holder to the named person.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a cheque with a receipt or a currency item

quiz.q: What do banks do with most of the money people deposit?
options: Keep all of it locked in the vault
Lend it out as loans, keeping only a small part as cash
quiz.explain: Banks keep a small portion as cash for withdrawals and use most deposits to give loans.
quiz.mistake: Thinks banks simply store all deposits

quiz.q: A bank pays 5% yearly interest on deposits and charges 9% yearly on loans. If it lends ₹1,00,000 of deposits for a year, how much does it earn from the difference?
quiz.explain: It earns ₹9,000 from the borrower and pays ₹5,000 to depositors, so it keeps ₹4,000.
steps: Interest earned = 9% of 1,00,000 = 9,000
Interest paid = 5% of 1,00,000 = 5,000
quiz.mistake: Gives only the interest earned and forgets the interest paid to depositors

teach.ask: Gappu has a pile of shiny pebbles: 'Why can't I just swap pebbles for seeds? Why do people need money?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Money is a medium of exchange, so we don't need a double coincidence of wants — and it's accepted because the government authorises it. Amazing!
teach.nudge: What problem does barter have? And why do people trust a paper note?

learn.hook: A loan can be a ladder that helps you climb — or a pit that is hard to climb out of!
points: Credit (a loan) is an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for a promise of future payment.

Credit can help: a potter borrows before Diwali to buy clay and colours, sells many diyas, repays and still earns a profit. Credit can also hurt: if a farmer's crop fails, she cannot repay and may have to sell land or borrow again. This is a debt trap.

Terms of credit include the interest rate, collateral, documentation and mode of repayment. Collateral is an asset the borrower owns — land, a building, a vehicle, livestock or bank deposits — kept as a guarantee; if the loan is not repaid, the lender can sell it.

Formal sources are banks and cooperatives. The Reserve Bank of India supervises them: it checks that banks keep enough cash, makes sure they lend to small farmers, small industries and small borrowers too, and collects information on whom they lend to and at what rate.

Informal sources are moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends. No organisation supervises them, so they may charge very high interest and use unfair ways to get money back. Higher interest means a bigger share of the borrower's earnings goes in repayment.

Rich households take most of their loans from formal sources, while poor households depend largely on informal sources — they often lack collateral and documents. So formal credit must expand, especially in rural areas, and reach the poor.

example.q: Think it through: Ravi borrows ₹10,000 for one year. A moneylender charges 5% per month; a bank charges 12% per year. How much more interest does he pay the moneylender?
steps: Moneylender: 5% of ₹10,000 = ₹500 per month; for 12 months = ₹6,000.
Bank: 12% of ₹10,000 for one year = ₹1,200.
The high informal interest eats a large part of Ravi's earnings.
example.answer: ₹4,800 more — formal credit is much cheaper.

learn.reallife: When a farmer in your village takes a crop loan from a bank or a cooperative society instead of a moneylender, she saves a lot on interest.

games.title: Formal or informal source?

quiz.explain: Collateral is an asset the borrower owns, such as land, a building, a vehicle or livestock, which the lender can sell if the loan is not repaid.
quiz.mistake: Thinks collateral can be something the borrower does not own

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the terms of credit?
quiz.explain: Terms of credit include interest rate, collateral, documentation and mode of repayment.

quiz.q: Ravi borrows ₹10,000 for 12 months. A moneylender charges 5% per month; a bank charges 12% per year. How much more interest would he pay the moneylender than the bank?
steps: Moneylender interest = 10,000 × 5/100 × 12 = 6,000
quiz.mistake: Gives the total moneylender interest instead of the difference

quiz.q: Shanti borrowed from a moneylender to grow crops. The crop failed, so she sold part of her land and borrowed again to repay. What is this situation called?
quiz.explain: When credit pushes a borrower into a situation from which recovery is very painful, it is called a debt trap.
quiz.mistake: Confuses debt trap with other money terms

quiz.q: Why do many poor households depend on informal sources of credit?
options: They often lack collateral and documents that banks ask for
Informal loans have the lowest interest rates
Banks are not allowed to lend to anyone in villages
The RBI asks them to borrow from moneylenders
quiz.explain: Without collateral and paperwork, the poor find bank loans hard to get, so they turn to moneylenders who know them personally.
quiz.mistake: Thinks informal credit is cheaper

teach.ask: Gappu wants to borrow worms from Uncle Crow: 'Is a loan good or bad? And why should I go to a bank instead of a moneylender?'
teach.praise: Hoot! Credit helps if you can repay, but can become a debt trap. Banks and cooperatives are cheaper and supervised by RBI, unlike moneylenders. Wonderful!
teach.nudge: What do lenders ask for as a guarantee? And why is a bank usually cheaper than a moneylender?

learn.hook: What if twenty neighbours could become their own little bank? That's the idea behind a Self-Help Group!
points: A Self-Help Group (SHG) typically has 15–20 members, usually women from the same neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly.
Members can take small loans from the group's own savings, at an interest rate lower than the moneylender's.

After a year or two, if the group saves regularly, it becomes eligible for a bank loan. The loan is sanctioned in the group's name and is meant to create self-employment — for example, to buy sewing machines, cattle or raw materials.

The group decides who gets a loan, how much, the interest and repayment. The group is responsible for repayment, and members follow up if someone does not repay. So banks are willing to lend to SHGs even without collateral.
SHGs help women become financially self-reliant, and their regular meetings let members discuss issues like health, nutrition and domestic violence.

Cooperatives also help: members such as farmers or weavers pool their resources; a farmers' cooperative accepts deposits from members, uses them as collateral to get a large bank loan, and lends to members. In Bangladesh, the Grameen Bank, started by Muhammad Yunus, has given credit to the poor at reasonable rates; Yunus and the Grameen Bank received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.

example.q: Think it through: Lakshmi has no land to offer as collateral. She wants ₹15,000 to buy a sewing machine. How can an SHG help her?
steps: Lakshmi joins an SHG of 18 women who save a small amount every month.
She can first borrow a small amount from the group's savings at low interest.
Once the group has saved regularly for a year or two, the bank gives it a loan without collateral.
The group lends Lakshmi ₹15,000; she stitches clothes, earns and repays in instalments.
example.answer: The SHG gives her access to cheap credit without collateral, helping her become self-employed.

learn.reallife: In many states, women's SHGs make pickles, papad, agarbattis or handicrafts and sell them at local melas — earning, saving and supporting one another.

quiz.q: How does a farmers' cooperative usually get a large loan from a bank?

quiz.mistake: Does not know how cooperatives pool resources

quiz.q: Who started the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh, which gives credit to the poor?
quiz.explain: Muhammad Yunus started the Grameen Bank; he and the bank received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.
quiz.mistake: Picks another well-known economist or scientist

teach.ask: Gappu and his sparrow friends want to start a nest-savings club: 'How does a Self-Help Group work, and why does it help the poor?'
teach.praise: Chirpy-chirp! Members save together, lend to each other, and later get bank loans without collateral because the group takes responsibility. Fantastic!
teach.nudge: What do SHG members do regularly? And why will a bank lend to them without collateral?

learn.hook: Your football may be designed in one country, stitched in another and sold in a third — all by one company!
points: Until about the middle of the 20th century, production was organised mostly within countries. What crossed borders were raw materials, food and finished goods. Colonies like India exported raw materials and food and imported finished goods.

A Multinational Corporation (MNC) is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation. MNCs set up offices and factories where they can get cheaper labour and other resources, to lower costs and earn more profit.
MNCs choose places that are close to markets, have skilled and unskilled labour at low cost, have other factors of production available, and have government policies that look after their interests.
Investment is money spent to buy assets such as land, buildings, machines and equipment. Investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment.

MNCs spread production by: setting up production jointly with local companies (bringing money for new machines and the latest technology); buying up local companies, which is the most common route; and placing orders with small producers, for example for garments, footwear and sports goods, which the MNC then sells under its own brand name.
Foreign trade connects markets: producers can sell beyond their own country, and buyers get more choice. For example, toys made in China are sold in Indian markets.

example.q: Think it through: A foreign company that makes mobile phones wants to open a factory in Asia. Why might it choose a city in India?
steps: India has a very large market of buyers close by.
It has many skilled engineers and workers at relatively low wages.
If roads, ports, power and government policies are favourable, costs fall further.
Lower costs and a big market mean higher profits for the MNC.
example.answer: Because of a large nearby market, low-cost skilled labour and supportive facilities and policies.

learn.reallife: Look at the label on your school bag, shoes or toy: 'Made in India' for a foreign brand, or 'Made in China' on a toy sold in your local market, shows production spread across countries.

games.title: Match the term
pairs: Owns or controls production in more than one nation
Money spent on land, buildings, machines and equipment
Most common route for MNC investment
MNC and a local company produce together

games.title: Would this attract an MNC?

quiz.q: What is a Multinational Corporation (MNC)?
options: A company that sells only in its home country

A government department that collects taxes
quiz.explain: An MNC's production is spread across more than one country.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'multinational' refers to many owners rather than many nations

quiz.q: Why do MNCs set up production in countries like India?
options: To get cheaper skilled labour and be close to large markets
Because they are forced to by the United Nations
Because there are no markets in their own countries
quiz.explain: Low-cost skilled labour and nearness to big markets reduce costs and increase profits.
quiz.mistake: Does not link MNC decisions to lower costs and profits

quiz.q: According to the textbook, what is the most common route for MNC investment?
options: Placing orders only with large government firms

quiz.mistake: Picks a different way of spreading production as the most common

quiz.q: What is 'foreign investment'?
options: Money Indians spend on foreign holidays
quiz.explain: Investment means buying assets like land, buildings and machines; when MNCs do it, it is foreign investment.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any spending abroad is foreign investment

quiz.q: A large foreign brand places orders with small garment makers in Tiruppur and sells the shirts under its own name. Which way of spreading production is this?
options: Placing orders for production with small producers
quiz.explain: The MNC does not own these units; it gets goods made by small producers and sells them under its brand.
quiz.mistake: Confuses placing orders with owning or buying companies

quiz.q: How can joint production with an MNC benefit a local Indian company?
options: It makes the local company pay no wages
It stops the local company from producing
The MNC can provide money for new machines and the latest technology
It closes the local company's market
quiz.explain: In joint production, the MNC brings additional investment, such as faster machines, and the latest technology.
quiz.mistake: Assumes partnership with an MNC only harms local firms

quiz.q: Before the middle of the 20th century, what did colonies like India mainly export?
quiz.explain: Colonies exported raw materials and food and imported finished goods.
quiz.mistake: Applies present-day exports to the colonial period

quiz.q: How does foreign trade help buyers?
options: It reduces the choice of goods
It makes all goods more expensive
It stops goods from other countries entering
It gives them a wider choice of goods beyond what is made at home
quiz.explain: Foreign trade brings goods from other countries, so buyers have more choice.
quiz.mistake: Thinks trade only benefits producers

teach.ask: Gappu found a toy with a foreign brand but 'Made in India' on it: 'How can that be? What is an MNC?'
teach.praise: Tweet! An MNC controls production in more than one country to cut costs and earn profits — by joint production, buying local firms or placing orders. Superb!
teach.nudge: In how many countries does an MNC produce? And why does it choose a particular country?

learn.hook: A call centre worker in Bengaluru can help a customer on another continent at midnight — welcome to a connected world!
points: Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries, mainly through more foreign trade and more foreign investment by MNCs. Goods, services, investments and technology move across countries; the movement of people is still limited.

Technology made it possible: faster and cheaper transport (containers carry goods on ships, trains, planes and trucks), and information and communication technology — telecommunications, computers and the internet. A magazine can be designed in Delhi and printed in Mumbai; call centres serve customers abroad.

A trade barrier is a restriction on trade set by the government, such as a tax on imports or a limit on how much can be imported. It lets the government decide which goods and how much of them enter the country.
After independence, India put barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment to protect its young industries from foreign competition.

Around 1991, India made big changes in its economic policy and removed barriers on trade and investment to a large extent. Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is called liberalisation. Indian producers now had to compete with foreign producers, which was expected to push them to improve quality.

example.q: Think it through: The government puts a heavy tax on imported toys. What happens to toy prices and to Indian toy makers?
steps: The import tax makes foreign toys costlier in Indian shops.
Fewer people buy imported toys.
Indian toy makers face less competition and sell more.
This is how a trade barrier protects domestic producers — and removing it (liberalisation) brings more competition.
example.answer: Imported toys become costlier, so Indian makers are protected; the tax is a trade barrier.

learn.reallife: Video calls with relatives working in the Gulf, or an online order shipped from another country, show how technology links people and markets across the world.

quiz.q: What is globalisation?
options: Rapid integration or interconnection between countries through trade and investment
Making goods only for the local market
Closing a country's borders to trade
quiz.explain: Globalisation links countries closely through more foreign trade and foreign investment by MNCs.
quiz.mistake: Confuses globalisation with protection or local trade

quiz.q: Under globalisation, the movement of which of these between countries is still limited?
quiz.explain: Goods, services, investment and technology move fairly freely, but countries still restrict the movement of people.
quiz.mistake: Assumes everything moves equally freely

quiz.q: Which development in technology has helped globalisation the most in services like call centres?
options: Information and communication technology, such as the internet
quiz.explain: Telecommunications, computers and the internet let services be provided instantly across countries.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the internet with global services

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of a trade barrier?
options: A bank loan to a farmer
quiz.explain: A tax on imports restricts trade by making foreign goods costlier.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything related to trade is a barrier

quiz.q: Why did India put barriers on foreign trade and investment after independence?
options: To protect domestic producers from foreign competition
Because there were no goods in the world
quiz.explain: Indian industries were just starting, so the government shielded them from strong foreign competition.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the aim of the barriers

quiz.q: Around which year did India remove barriers on foreign trade and investment to a large extent?
quiz.explain: Major changes in economic policy were made around 1991.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 1991 with independence or other years

quiz.q: What does 'liberalisation' mean?
options: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government
quiz.explain: Liberalisation means freeing trade and investment from government restrictions.
quiz.mistake: Confuses liberalisation with protection or nationalisation

quiz.q: What did liberalisation mean for Indian producers?
options: They no longer had any competition
They had to compete with foreign producers, which pushed them to improve quality
They had to close all their factories
quiz.explain: With barriers removed, foreign goods entered India, so Indian producers faced competition and had to improve.
quiz.mistake: Thinks removing barriers reduces competition

teach.ask: Gappu read the word 'liberalisation' in a newspaper: 'Is it about birds being set free? What happened in 1991?'
teach.praise: Chirrup! Liberalisation means removing government barriers on trade and investment — India did this around 1991, and technology sped up globalisation. Excellent!
teach.nudge: What are trade barriers, and what did India do with them around 1991?

topics.title: WTO, impact of globalisation and fair globalisation

learn.hook: Globalisation is like a big cricket tournament — great if the rules are fair for every team, not just the strongest!
points: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) aims to liberalise international trade. Started at the initiative of developed countries, it sets rules for international trade and checks that they are obeyed.

Critics say WTO rules have been unfair: developed countries have kept their own trade barriers while pushing developing countries to remove theirs. The textbook's example: the US government gives large sums of money to its farmers, so they can sell farm products abroad at very low prices, which hurts farmers in developing countries.

Who gained in India: well-off consumers (more choice, better quality, lower prices); MNCs increased investment in mobile phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food and banking in cities; local companies supplying MNCs; some large Indian companies became MNCs themselves; IT service companies got new opportunities.

Who faced difficulties: many small producers — for example of batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products and vegetable oil — faced tough competition and some shut down. Many workers now get only temporary, flexible jobs with long hours and little security.

To attract foreign companies, the government set up Special Economic Zones (SEZs) with world-class facilities — electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, recreation and education. According to the textbook, companies setting up units in SEZs do not pay taxes for an initial period of five years.

Fair globalisation creates opportunities for all and shares the benefits better. The government can make sure labour laws are followed, support small producers, use trade and investment barriers if needed, and join other developing countries to bargain for fairer WTO rules. People's organisations and campaigns can also make a difference.

example.q: Think it through: Cheap imported toys flood the market. Small toy makers in a town are losing business. What could make globalisation fairer for them?
steps: Consumers gain from cheaper toys, but the small producers lose income.
The government could help small makers improve quality and lower costs with cheap credit and better technology.
If needed, it could use a trade barrier, such as an import tax, to give them time to become competitive.
It could also negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules for developing countries.
example.answer: Support small producers, use barriers where needed, and bargain for fair rules — so benefits are shared by all.

learn.reallife: Wooden toys from Channapatna in Karnataka and Etikoppaka in Andhra Pradesh compete with imported toys; support for such small producers is part of making globalisation fair.

games.title: WTO and fair globalisation: true or false?
items: The WTO aims to liberalise international trade.
Its rules are meant to reduce barriers to trade between countries.
The WTO was started at the initiative of developing countries.
It was started at the initiative of developed countries.
Some developed countries have kept trade barriers while asking developing countries to remove theirs.
This is a key reason why WTO rules are called unfair.
Every person in India gained equally from globalisation.
Well-off consumers and big companies gained more; many small producers and workers faced difficulties.
According to the textbook, companies setting up units in SEZs do not pay taxes for an initial period of five years.
The textbook describes this tax benefit as a way to attract companies to SEZs.
Fair globalisation means benefits are shared by all, not just a few.
It aims to create opportunities for everyone.

quiz.q: What is the main aim of the World Trade Organisation (WTO)?
options: To issue currency for all countries
To build roads in developing countries
quiz.explain: The WTO sets rules to reduce barriers in international trade and makes sure they are followed.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the WTO with banks or development agencies

quiz.q: At whose initiative was the WTO started?
quiz.explain: The WTO was set up at the initiative of developed countries.
quiz.mistake: Assumes it was started by developing countries

quiz.q: Why are WTO rules often said to be unfair to developing countries?
options: Developed countries have kept their own trade barriers while pushing developing countries to remove theirs
Developing countries are not allowed to export anything
The WTO gives all its money to poor countries
quiz.explain: Developed countries, for example through large farm subsidies, protect their producers while developing countries are asked to open up.
quiz.mistake: Misses the double standard in trade rules

quiz.q: The textbook mentions that the US government gives large sums to its farmers. What is the effect on farmers in developing countries?
options: They get higher prices for their crops
They receive the same money from the US
They lose out, because cheap US farm products lower the prices they can get
quiz.explain: Subsidised US farmers can sell at very low prices, so farmers in developing countries struggle to compete.
quiz.mistake: Does not see how subsidies abroad affect prices for other farmers

quiz.q: Which group of consumers has benefited most from globalisation in India?
quiz.explain: Well-off urban consumers enjoy more choice, better quality and lower prices.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up consumers who gained with producers who lost

quiz.q: According to the textbook, for how long are companies that set up units in SEZs exempt from taxes?
quiz.explain: Companies in Special Economic Zones do not pay taxes for an initial period of five years.
quiz.mistake: Guesses the period instead of recalling the five-year tax holiday

quiz.q: What does 'fair globalisation' mean?
options: Only developed countries should set the rules
It should create opportunities for all and share the benefits better
quiz.explain: Fair globalisation aims for everyone, including small producers and workers, to benefit.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fairness means stopping trade or helping only the powerful

quiz.q: Which government step would help make globalisation fairer?
options: Ignoring labour laws so companies can save money
Removing all support for small producers
Ensuring labour laws are properly implemented so workers get their rights
Letting developed countries alone decide trade rules
quiz.explain: Proper labour laws protect workers, which helps share the benefits of globalisation more fairly.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a step that would increase unfairness

teach.ask: Gappu is worried: 'My cousin's small toy shop is losing to cheap imported toys. Is globalisation good or bad? What can make it fair?'
teach.praise: Hurray! Globalisation helped some and hurt others; fair rules at the WTO, labour laws and support for small producers can share the benefits with all. Brilliant!
teach.nudge: Who gained and who lost from globalisation? And what can the government do to make it fair?
